title: Cube
intro: Cube starts with an apparently complete answer to other people: they are ungrateful and cannot be trusted. It ends by admitting that people have many sides and remain hard to understand after years. Between those positions, betrayal produces threats, warnings and fantasies of punishment. Even the claim that heaven will deal with an enemy does not last; the speaker soon wants a lighter himself. The cube leaves the hurt unresolved. Naming someone a monster can protect you from them without explaining the person you thought you knew.
reading: Repetitive certainty about betrayal gives way to inability to understand many-sided people; delegated justice repeatedly becomes personal revenge.

revisions.10-wolf: The opening repeats a verdict until it seems to leave no room for qualification. A white-eyed wolf is someone who repays care with betrayal, so the accusation already contains a damaged relationship: something was given before trust was broken. The ending complicates this certainty by admitting that people have many sides. The insult may express the injury accurately without providing the complete explanation the speaker keeps searching for.
revisions.phrase-10-heart: The warning against opening your heart follows a threat built from information supplied by little friends. Intimacy has become a route through which someone can be found and hurt. That gives the general advice a specific mechanism: people become dangerous because they know things about you. The speaker then turns his experience into a lesson for others, even though the final refrain admits that experience has still not made people intelligible to him.
revisions.10-evil: The proverb promises that a bad person will meet another bad person capable of punishing them. 'I do not need to act' briefly hands the problem over to a larger moral order. But the following funeral-property fantasy and borrowed lighter bring the speaker back into the punishment scene. He cannot quite maintain the distance he announces. The movement between leaving it to heaven and doing it himself is part of the anger's instability.
revisions.editorial-10-lighter: Borrowing a lighter sounds like the start of a mundane smoking interaction. He explicitly rejects that purpose and enlarges it into arson. The small social request makes the violent turn comic and disturbing at once. More importantly, it reverses the preceding claim that he need not lift a hand: the imagination keeps recruiting him back into revenge. This is a performed escalation, not evidence that the lyric records an actual fire.
revisions.10-sides: The many-sided person and the repeated cube image replace the opening's one-word judgement with a problem that has not been solved. Years of knowing someone have not made all their sides visible together. The long repetition does not demonstrate a solution; it keeps turning the object over. That is why the ending feels different from a generic statement that people are complicated: it arrives after the speaker has spent the song trying to make betrayal morally simple.
